title: Is a lowball offer worth taking?
hook: Say no and you both get nothing. Turning down an insult feels right. Does it pay?

doesNotKnow: that a money-only responder should accept any positive offer

misconception: A rational responder rejects an insulting offer.
objective: The learner can explain why a responder who counts only money accepts any offer above $0, and so why a proposer facing one offers the smallest unit.

claims.text: If you reject, you and the proposer both get $0; if you accept an offer of $X out of $10, you get $X and the proposer keeps $10 − X.
claims.source: The rules of the ultimatum game as set on the card (whole dollars, $10 pot). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Rules as coded (POT 10, whole dollars; Accept cell (X, 10 - X), Reject (0, 0)).

claims.text: A responder who cares only about money prefers $1 to $0, so accepts any positive offer; the smallest offer worth accepting is $1, and at $0 accepting and rejecting come out the same.
claims.source: Compare accept ($X) with reject ($0): X > 0 for X ≥ 1; X = 0 is a tie. Demo.tsx accepts() and SMALLEST; re-run in node by the builder (ncm-e02). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): accepts(offer) = offer > 0; SMALLEST = 1; offer 0 shows the tie ring and '$0 either way'. Predict answer index resolves to '$1'.

claims.text: Rejecting a $1 offer costs the proposer $9 but costs you the $1 too, so for a money-only responder it is a pure loss.
claims.source: From c1 at X = 1: accept gives (1, 9), reject gives (0, 0). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): X = 1: accept (1, 9), reject (0, 0). Reveal quotes POT - SMALLEST = 9.

claims.text: A proposer who knows the responder counts only money offers $1 and keeps $9.
claims.source: Backward induction: every offer of $1 or more is accepted (c2), so the proposer's best accepted offer is the smallest unit, $1 of $10, keeping $9. (Offering $0 leaves the responder indifferent, so it is not a sure acceptance.) | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Backward induction with a sure-acceptance proposer. Note: in the discrete game an equilibrium where $0 is offered and accepted also exists; the sentence does not say 'only', and the source states the tie. Easley-Kleinberg ch. 12 (bargaining, ultimatum game) placement matches my knowledge; book not opened.

claims.text: This is a model that counts only money; if a responder also cares about fairness, saying no can make sense, and that is a different model.
claims.source: Lesson framing; stage chip 'Model: you care only about money · whole dollars'. Experimental offer and rejection rates (brief claim 3: Güth, Schmittberger and Schwarze 1982; Camerer 2003) need a human source check and are kept out of learner text. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Framing; stage chip and reveal muted line match. Experimental rates correctly kept out of learner text.

recall.question: A proposer splits $20 in whole dollars. If the responder says no, both get nothing. Against a responder who counts only money, what should the proposer offer?
recall.why: Any amount above $0 beats the $0 from rejecting, so a money-only responder takes $1, and the proposer keeps $19.
